paragraphs: The following judgments concern materials engineers' engineering and research practices. They do not predict hiring, registration, qualification, or contract outcomes.

The core work of materials engineers is to ensure materials meet product requirements within cost and performance constraints: conduct or supervise raw-material and finished-product tests to ensure quality; recommend materials against design goals such as strength, weight, heat resistance, conductivity, and cost; evaluate technical and economic factors in processes and product designs; plan laboratories and develop materials and manufacturing processes; analyze product failure data and test results to determine causes and propose solutions; determine manufacturing and joining methods; design and direct process tests; monitor material performance and deterioration; and reproduce material characteristics and train customers when needed.

Entirely fictional task package: provide fictional material performance data and failure examples, including 1 set of design requirements and selection constraints, 1 set of test data and failure observations, and 1 selection trade-off problem. Within 60 minutes, write testing and evaluation approaches, candidate materials and process options, failure-cause hypotheses and validation methods, and risks. Do not use real company, product, or classified data.

Sample output and reflection: check whether design requirements and constraints were defined first, data sources and test conditions were explained, comparable material and process options were provided, and validation and failure-analysis boundaries were stated. Then ask yourself whether you can balance performance, processes, and cost, communicate across design, manufacturing, and quality teams, and take responsibility for material conclusions and consequences.

On this page, materials engineers refers to O*NET 17-2131.00: workers who evaluate materials and develop machinery and processes to manufacture materials for products meeting specific design and performance specifications, and develop new uses for known materials, including titles such as metallurgical engineer, ceramic engineer, and welding engineer. Tasks include testing raw materials and finished products, recommending materials against design goals, assessing technical and economic factors, planning laboratories and developing materials and manufacturing processes, analyzing failure data, determining manufacturing and joining methods, designing and directing process tests, monitoring material performance and deterioration, and reproducing material characteristics. Work mainly takes place in laboratories, factories, and offices. This page excludes adjacent roles such as architectural and engineering managers, biomedical engineers, chemical engineers, electrical engineers, and electronics engineers.

entries: Inputs: design and performance requirements, materials and alloy systems, test and inspection equipment, process and joining methods, failure and deterioration data, cost and capacity constraints, regulatory and safety requirements, stakeholders, and project goals.

Checkable outputs: material selection and substitution recommendations, test plans and data conclusions, failure analyses and improvement options, process and joining methods, performance and deterioration assessments, technical reports and budget proposals, and training and material-transfer documentation.

Complete workflow: define design and performance requirements → collect material and test data → evaluate selection and process options → perform testing and failure analysis → propose improvement and validation plans → support trial and mass production.

paragraphs: Key judgments: whether design requirements and test conditions are clear, data and failure conclusions are reliable, selection and processes balance performance, cost, and safety, improvements can be validated, and conclusions exceed engineering and authorization boundaries.

Environment and pace: primarily controlled indoor settings, including laboratories and factory sites. Work involves extensive email and meeting communication, prolonged test analysis and documentation, and an emphasis on precision. Workers may encounter contaminants, hazardous conditions, and equipment and bear safety responsibility.

Research inputs: occupational identity, tasks, work activities, work context, skills and knowledge, interest code, education, and Job Zone for O*NET 17-2131.00. Wage, employment, and industry data on that page cover this occupation. Research conclusions do not establish mainland China's qualification, wage, or employment scope.

Check first: design requirements and performance indicators, test conditions and data scope, material and process constraints, cost and capacity limits, safety and compliance requirements, and evidence strength and authorization boundaries for conclusions.

End-to-end work: define design and performance requirements, collect data, evaluate selection and processes, conduct tests and failure analysis, propose improvements and validation, and support trial and mass production. Do not conclude before test conditions or data scope are confirmed, or put materials into use before safety and compliance boundaries are checked.

Boundaries with adjacent roles: this page covers only materials engineers. Architectural and engineering managers oversee projects and teams; biomedical engineers handle medical engineering; chemical engineers handle chemical processes; electrical engineers handle electrical systems; electronics engineers handle electronic devices and circuits. Professional judgments and authorizations are not interchangeable with this occupation.
Architectural and engineering managers oversee projects, teams, and budgets; materials engineers handle material selection, testing, and process development. Responsibilities differ.

Biomedical engineers work with medical and biological engineering; materials engineers work with materials and manufacturing processes. Medical materials require collaboration with biomedical engineering.

Chemical engineers handle chemical processes and plants; materials engineers handle material performance, selection, and manufacturing processes. The roles overlap in material processing but have different goals.

Electrical engineers handle electrical systems and equipment; materials engineers handle materials and processes. Conclusions on electrically functional materials require collaboration with electrical engineering.
Boundaries of AI's impact on materials engineers

Editorial task hypothesis: distinguish materials simulation, machine learning for performance prediction, and generative AI. The latter may help organize fictional test records, literature summaries, or report drafts. No occupational adoption rates / job outcomes were obtained. Model output is not measured performance. People must verify original conditions, data, standards applicability, and citations. Do not upload formulations or client secrets without approval or release materials based on generated text.

Occupational sources describe actual tasks and subjects: materials and alloys, tests and equipment, processes and joining, failures and performance. Tool capabilities, organizational adoption, and job outcomes are recorded separately; wage or employment data is not used as AI evidence.

Editorial comparison: drafts may receive assistance, but no adoption-sequencing research was obtained. Traditional simulation / machine learning does not demonstrate generative AI adoption or product safety. Selection / failure causality requires experimental validation.

Human control points: define design and performance requirements, judge test conditions and data reliability, balance performance, processes, and costs, take responsibility for failure conclusions and safety compliance, and follow engineering ethics and authorization boundaries.

First conduct an offline exercise using entirely fictional material performance data and failure examples. Write testing and evaluation approaches, selection options, and validation boundaries without relying on unverified automated analysis to replace engineering judgment.
Editorial hypothesis: documentation may receive assistance. Specialized calculation and generative text capabilities differ; adoption or replacement has not been demonstrated.

Retain specimen / batch information, test conditions, and original results, and check model applicability and citations. Do not release unvalidated performance or sign beyond your authority; hand over instead.

Insufficient evidence: this research did not obtain a Chinese occupational wage distribution safely matching 17-2131.00. Existing manufacturing-unit averages provide only manufacturing employer context; check research and development / engineering service employers separately. They are not occupational medians and do not imply public data does not exist.

US wage and employment scope for materials engineers, occupation 17-2131.00

The 2025 US median wage for 17-2131 is 112,860 dollars annually and 54.26 dollars hourly; full percentiles appear in the table. Older employment of 23,000 in 2024 and 1,500 average annual openings in 2024—2034 are separate. Latest figures are 23,800 employed in 2025, 8% growth in 2025—2035, and 1,300 average annual openings. Net growth and replacement openings differ; these are not individual hiring probabilities.
2025 US nationwide occupational wages for 17-2131. Annual and hourly percentiles are entered separately from the original table, not as a conversion of individual working hours or take-home income.
P10/25/50/75/90 denotes wage distribution positions, not beginner / senior levels. Interpret employment size, openings, and individual opportunities separately.

BLS May 2025 occupational industry median annual wages: 137,610 dollars in government excluding state and local education and hospitals, 132,070 in natural sciences / engineering / life sciences research and development, 125,190 in transportation equipment manufacturing, and 124,950 in engineering services. These are occupational wages within industries, not averages for all industry personnel or employment shares.

The older 1,500 figure is average annual openings in 2024—2034, not a period total. The newer 2025—2035 annual average of 1,300 includes replacements; do not mix it with approximately 1,800 net new jobs or current vacancies.
Fit signals: start with observable work behavior

To assess fit, consider whether you can translate product requirements into material and test plans, rigorously analyze test and failure data, balance performance, processes, and cost, communicate across design, manufacturing, and quality teams, and keep learning materials and standards. Tools such as RIASEC can only propose hypotheses and cannot replace real task experience.

Positive signals: structured materials analysis, data- and test-based judgment, selection trade-offs under multiple constraints, communication and coordination across parties, and responsibility for conclusions and safety.

Reasons for caution: difficulty quantifying design requirements, skipping testing and data validation, unwillingness to communicate and advance work between laboratories and factories, or difficulty handling safety and compliance pressure.
Trial activity: using entirely fictional material performance data and failure examples, rehearse selection, evaluation, and failure analysis, and ask someone else to review them against the records.

The O*NET interest code is RIC (Realistic–Investigative–Conventional), emphasizing hands-on practice, research and analysis, and organizing information according to procedures. These labels describe activity preferences only and cannot determine competence or qualifications.

General personality measures such as the Big Five do not provide job evidence for this occupation and can only support self-reflection. Continue checking through real material testing, failure analysis, and selection communication experiences.
Type-based tools such as MBTI and the Enneagram cannot determine competence or qualifications and can only support self-reflection.

Material selection and performance noncompliance risks
Process and joining feasibility risks
Safety and hazardous-condition exposure risks
Conclusion authorization and compliance-boundary risks
Entry pathways and capability stages

ONet's new-hire education survey reports 80% bachelor's, 8% doctorate, and 4% two-year / associate degree, not a uniform threshold. Years of preparation for JobZone4 is a group description. BLS says entry typically requires a materials or related engineering bachelor's; some research and development roles require a master's or doctorate. Entry does not require prior years of related work or a PE.

US materials / related engineering bachelor's study with laboratory and project practice; some research and development positions require a master's or doctorate. A PE is not required for entry. Check public services / project sign-off under state law and specific authorization. No exact unified Chinese qualification match was established. Actual welding, nondestructive testing, or special equipment work requires separate checks of applicable regulatory categories and qualifications; a materials engineering degree does not automatically confer them.

Education, professional certification, and practice / special-operation qualifications, such as welding, nondestructive testing, and special equipment qualifications, are different statuses. A degree or certification does not automatically grant operating qualifications. Statutory sign-offs and safety conclusions must be issued by appropriately qualified personnel or organizations.

Entry stage: practice materials and testing fundamentals, data recording and analysis, basic failure observation, learning processes and standards, and documentation under supervision. Learn safety and compliance requirements and retain process records.

Evidence to show: use a reviewable material or process deliverable covering requirements definition, test conditions, data conclusions, and selection recommendations to demonstrate structured engineering analysis and accurate documentation.

Next step: check the target employer's material systems and processes, standards and compliance requirements, and testing and inspection conditions. Validate testing, analysis, and selection abilities through real projects under supervision.

Moving toward greater responsibility: with experience, workers may oversee end-to-end material or process development, train newcomers and establish systematic methods, or move into research and development management, quality, and process engineering.
Market signals and transition directions

Retain older employment of 23,000 in 2024 and 1,500 average annual openings in 2024—2034. Latest figures are 23,800 employed in 2025, 8% growth in 2025—2035, and 1,300 average annual openings, including replacements, not ten-year totals, net new jobs, or individual hiring probabilities.

The main industries on that page for 2024 are Manufacturing and Professional, Scientific, and Technical Services. Employment and openings are statistical projections and must be interpreted separately from individual opportunities.

Transferable capabilities: material and test analysis, failure analysis and root-cause judgments, process and joining methods, data and standards interpretation, cost and performance trade-offs, interdisciplinary communication, and project management.

First target, architectural and engineering manager: add research and development / project planning, personnel and equipment allocation, budgets, hiring and team leadership, and quality and schedule coordination. Technical competence in material testing does not automatically demonstrate management responsibility or authorization across engineering disciplines. Build real resource and team deliverables for the target role.

source_card.note: Source scope, limitations, and statistical periods are checked separately against the original evidence. Source use notes: O*NET 17-2131.00 Materials Engineers (Summary): Provides the occupational identity, official description, interest code, Job Zone, skills, and knowledge for 17-2131.00.; The wage and employment data on that page cover this occupation.; O*NET 17-2131.00 Tasks: Provides a task list including testing raw materials and finished products, recommending material choices based on design objectives, evaluating technical and economic factors, planning laboratories and developing materials and processes, analyzing failure data, determining manufacturing and joining methods, and monitoring material performance.; The task sample does not mean every position performs every task.; O*NET 17-2131.00 Work Context: Describes settings that are primarily controlled indoor environments, daily communication by email and meetings, an emphasis on precision, and possible exposure to contaminants, hazardous conditions, and equipment.; U.S. work context does not replace Chinese law or employer procedures.; O*NET 17-2131.00 National Wages (BLS OEWS display): Median wage from 2025 BLS OEWS; the page covers this occupation.; Percentile wages are not displayed on this page.; O*NET 17-2131.00 National Employment Trends: Employment size in 2024, growth in 2024–2034 (faster than average at 5%–6%), and projected job openings.; Projections are not hiring guarantees.; Industries: 17-2131.00: The main industries on this page for 2024 are Manufacturing and Professional, Scientific, and Technical Services.; Industry distribution signals employer settings, not projected growth or demand.; O*NET 17-2131.00 Education and Career Preparation: Job Zone 4: Most positions require a four-year bachelor's degree (about 80%), while some require a doctorate (about 8%) or a two-year degree.; The education distribution does not constitute a mandatory requirement for every employer.; Licenses & Certifications: 17-2131.00: State licensing and national certification search tools provided by O*NET.; Certification and training do not equal authorization to practice or employer hiring requirements.; Generative AI and Jobs (ILO Working Paper 140, 2025): Assesses occupational exposure to generative AI at the task level.; The exposure index does not equal adoption rates, job outcomes, or hiring probabilities.; Average Annual Wages of Persons Employed in Urban Units in 2025: Provides average annual wages by broad industry category for urban non-private and private units, including manufacturing.; An industry average is not an occupational median and excludes individual businesses and freelancers.; FermatMind Materials Engineers Task Impact Scale: Organizes tasks that can be assisted and points requiring human control for task-level discussions of AI and fit.; This editorial scale is not evidence of adoption rates, layoffs, regulations, or licensing.;
